transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-05-19
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Dana (Aurelia Head of Platform), Tom (Aurelia SRE), Priya (Aurelia ML)
Links shared: Deck: https://drive.redwood/demo/aurelia-chat-smoke.pdf, Benchmark sheet (view only): https://sheets.redwood/bench-aurelia

Summary:
Quick hands-on demo focused on chat/text gen basics with live streaming, parameter tuning, and retry / fallback grid. Customer emphasized low-latency 95th pctl and strict data residency / SOC2 requirements. POC planned to run small benchmark using their prompt set.

Topics Covered:
- Streaming behaviour and how to surface partial tokens to UI
- Timeout & retry strategies (idempotency, backoff, no-dup generation)
- Param choices (max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop sequences) for throughput vs quality tradeoffs
- KV cache / prefix caching and how it reduces cost for repeated contexts
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs VPC/private tradeoffs (latency predictability and data isolation)
- Security: SOC2, KMS/HSM, SAML SSO, audit logs

Transcript:
[00:00:06] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're gonna run through a short live walk and then a quick smoke benchmark, try not to be too formal, call it a lab demo, okay?
[00:00:18] Dana: Sounds good, we've got about 45 minutes, we want to validate latency and retry behavior for our chat assistant used in clinical triage, so 95th percentile matters.
[00:00:30] Marco: Quick intro, I'm Marco, I'm the SE on this account, I'll show the console and then jump into a tiny load script for streaming.
[00:00:38] Tom: Quick note — we care about data not leaving our VPC, can you restate the private deployment options, we heard about Private Control Plane earlier.
[00:00:47] Sofia: Yes, absolutely; we have Hosted API for rapid start, Dedicated reserved capacity for predictable throughput, and Redwood Private which can be VPC peering/on-prem. For the POC we can do hosted but with client-side encryption and audit logs; if you need full network isolation we'll plan a Private deployment.
[00:01:05] Priya: Are there inline KMS options? We need per-tenant key separation.
[00:01:10] Marco: Yes, we integrate KMS/HSM — customers can bring keys via their cloud KMS and we support envelope encryption; in Private you can host the control plane.
[00:01:20] Dana: Ok great, can we jump into streaming? We want to understand partial token latencies and how retries interact with streams.

[00:01:31] Marco: Sure — for streaming we push partial chunks as tokens arrive, you get low time-to-first-byte and a continuous event stream. Here's a quick console demo — I'm opening the gen sandbox.
[00:01:46] [screen share noise / short pause]
[00:01:51] Marco: Alright I'm calling the chat endpoint with streaming enabled, you can see the first chunk at about 120ms for a short prompt — that's typical on our fastest regions. In this particular region though we're at 130ms — network wobble.
[00:02:08] Tom: That 120-130ms is great. What's the difference when batching / concurrency increases?
[00:02:14] Marco: Good question — when we batch, tail latency for an individual request can increase, but tokens-per-dollar improves. We have automatic batching heuristics and you can set max_batch_size and latency SLOs. If your client needs consistent p95 under 300ms we recommend smaller batch caps and enable prefix caching where possible.
[00:02:33] Priya: Can you explain prefix caching? We saw 'KV cache' in the docs but uncertain how it maps to conversation histories.
[00:02:39] Marco: KV cache stores the transformer key/value cache for recent prefixes; for chat apps repeated system prompts or common context can be served from cache avoiding recomputation. In practice you get dramatic savings for long contexts with stable prefixes. Note transcription note: sometimes our transcript says KV "cash" — it's 'cache'.
[00:02:59] Dana: Does caching affect correctness? If we change the prompt we need to invalidate cache, right?
[00:03:04] Marco: Exactly, the platform exposes TTLs and explicit invalidation calls. We also support prefix fingerprinting — you can key cache entries on a hash of the prefix so when you change content it's a new cache key.
[00:03:15] Sofia: Back to retries — common pattern is a client-level retry with idempotency token. We provide an idempotency key per request and a recommended backoff policy. Marco, show the retry grid.
[00:03:27] Marco: Right, in the console we have a retry/playbook tab — it lists transient vs hard errors. For transient infra errors we do exponential backoff and incremental model fallback. For example if the preferred model is a high-perf gpt-ish variant and it fails, we can fallback to a slightly cheaper quantized variant automatically.
[00:03:45] Tom: How do you avoid duplicate chunks when retrying a streaming request? We can't show duplicate suggestions to clinicians.
[00:03:51] Marco: The client flow: you retry with the same idempotency key and the service returns the last committed token offset; the client resumes streaming from there. That prevents duplication. In older transcripts this part sometimes gets blurred as 'resume from token off set' — but the mechanism is robust.
[00:04:10] Priya: If a model fallback happens, do you get notification that the model changed so we can record that in our logs?
[00:04:15] Marco: Yes, we emit a trace event with model_version and fallback_reason. Console and the trace API surface it; the Optimize toolkit can correlate quality regressions with fallback events.
[00:04:27] Dana: On cost — what's the unit economics tradeoff for keeping long contexts cached vs recompute?
[00:04:32] Marco: If you can cache the first N tokens, you avoid re-decoding the same KV and you save tokens billed for generation compute. Savings are workload-dependent; our Optimize suggestions show predicted cost delta when enabling prefix caching.
[00:04:46] Dana: We're concerned about hallucination in clinical prompts; we need confidence scoring and reranks. Any quick notes?
[00:04:53] Marco: We have an embeddings + rerank pattern and a calibrated confidence wrapper that you can run post-generation; Optimize can run eval sets and alert on regression. For clinical use the pattern is: generate, run an information retrieval check and rerank outputs, then apply guardrails.
[00:05:07] Tom: Security again — audit logs and retention — can we set retention window and ensure logs are exported to our SIEM?
[00:05:13] Sofia: Yes, audit logs can be streamed to your logging endpoint (we support syslog/forwarder or cloud storage) and retention windows are configurable for Private; hosted has standard retention but enterprise tier allows longer retention or S3 exports.
[00:05:25] Priya: Great. Can we run a small smoke benchmark now? Maybe 100 concurrent lightweight prompts and observe p50/p95 for streaming first byte and overall generation?
[00:05:33] Marco: Yep — I'll kick off a small load run from the sandbox. I'll also toggle max_tokens and temperature to show differences.
[00:05:41] [background typing / small noise]
[00:05:48] Marco: Running test: 100 concurrent, prompt set from demo scenario. First-byte p50: 115ms, p95: 280ms here in our region. Generation complete p95 roughly 420ms for a short response. That aligns with our expectations for that instance type.
[00:06:08] Dana: Good, can you toggle batching to emulate our bursty traffic?
[00:06:13] Marco: Switching to medium batching, increasing max_batch_size to 8, target latency SLO 200ms. Re-run.
[00:06:22] [pause / small lag]
[00:06:27] Marco: Ok now p50 140ms, p95 560ms — tokens-per-dollar improved about 1.8x but p95 increased. That's the tradeoff.
[00:06:40] Tom: That's useful; for triage we can accept higher mean latency but p95 must be < 800ms. Looks doable.
[00:06:47] Priya: Can we simulate retries? I want to see a transient error and how client resumes.
[00:06:52] Marco: I'll inject a transient worker failure in the sandbox, force a 503 for some requests.
[00:06:58] [keyboard clack, short audio artifact]
[00:07:04] Marco: Triggering failure now — you'll see some requests hit 503 and the client library does exponential backoff. The resume semantics are visible in the trace: it resumes from token offset 42 for one of the requests.
[00:07:16] [slight crosstalk]
[00:07:20] Dana: In that resume trace, do we get any partial output duplicates in the UI?
[00:07:24] Marco: No duplicates — the idempotency+offset protocol ensures no dupes. We'll share the trace JSON after the call.
[00:07:31] Priya: One more — how are stop sequences handled in streaming? If a stop token occurs mid-stream do you close gracefully?
[00:07:36] Marco: The runtime ceases generation and streams a final 'done' event; client binds that to finalize the message. There's a small race if you have streaming + client-side stitching, but the SDKs provide helpers to handle it.
[00:07:48] Sofia: Quick question from Dana in chat: do you have an example of a canary rollout and automatic fallback?
[00:07:54] Marco: Yes, in the console's rollout page you can create a canary that sends X% of traffic to new model version. We have policies to auto-fallback if error rate or latency breaches thresholds.
[00:08:04] Dana: If we do POC on hosted and later want Private, how disruptive is the migration?
[00:08:09] Sofia: We try to keep the API surface identical — you can pin model versions and rollout configs. Migration planning focuses on transfer of keys, network config and any on-prem infra. We've done multiple customers with near-zero client changes.
[00:08:21] Tom: Any caveats for latency when moving to VPC peering? We've seen added 20-40ms.
[00:08:27] Marco: Yes, peering and cross-region hops add measurable latency; we can recommend co-located regions and dedicated capacity for tighter SLOs.
[00:08:35] Priya: For the POC, can Optimize give recommendations like "set quantized model + batch x for better cost"?
[00:08:41] Marco: Exactly — Optimize runs against your workload traces, suggests model family (float16 vs int8/q4) and batch settings. It can even produce expected cost numbers.
[00:08:51] Sofia: Ok, let's recap logistics: we'll send a sandbox invite, you (Aurelia) will provision prompts and targets, and we'll schedule a 2-hour POC next week.
[00:08:59] Dana: That works. A couple final quick Qs — can you share SOC2 and maybe a short compliance summary for healthcare?
[00:09:05] Sofia: Yes will send SOC2 plus HIPAA-adjacent notes; full HIPAA support is available on the Private plan, with BAAs — we'll surface that in the doc.
[00:09:14] Tom: Great. Also would like an export of the console traces for the replay — that helps our SREs.
[00:09:19] Marco: I'll export the trace bundle and drop it in the shared sheet.
[00:09:24] Priya: Any competitor comparison notes? We evaluated Anthropic and Bedrock — curious on multi-region replication.
[00:09:30] Sofia: Redwood focuses on runtime consistency and cost controls; many providers are model-first. That said, we integrate common model families and emphasize deployment flex. We'll send a short competitor note.
[00:09:40] Dana: Fantastic. Thanks.
[00:09:42] Sofia: Thanks all — I'll send the next steps and the invite for the POC.

[00:09:48] End of main demo — wrap / housekeeping / small chitchat (music? noise)

Recap / Decisions / Next Steps:
- POC: 2-hour sandbox benchmark session to run with Aurelia prompt set (target week of 2026-05-25).
- Security docs: Redwood to send SOC2 + compliance summary + BAA options for Private.
- Benchmarks: Marco to provision sandbox and run KV cache + batching permutations; results to be uploaded to shared sheet.

Action Items (restate):

Notes about transcription quality: there are a few mis-heard terms in the live transcript (e.g., 'KV cash' -> KV cache, 'resume token off set' -> resume token offset). Speaker attribution mostly accurate though short crosstalk occurred.
